utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No -- yes. I do understand that the Prosecution wanted to raise one preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, everyone. I just managed to speak to Mr. Stojanovic about a small matter that in -- we have made a -- the Prosecution has put together a small booklet which is an index of the Srebrenica intercepts, just a real brief summary of what they say by chronology, along with a DVD or a CD of the actual intercepts. It's something that we have provided the Defence in both languages, and something we -- I traditionally provide to the Court, not as evidence because it's all in evidence already, but just as something that may help you. Mr. Stojanovic has agreed that, should you wish, we can provide that and we have copies upstairs for you, if you would like it. And so we -- we offer this, present this this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, no objection that this little aid will be given to the Chamber, and in the full understanding that it doesn't add anything to the evidence but that it just is kind of a road map through the evidence in relation to those intercepts. If that is clear and accepted by the parties then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right, and we can bring that down tomorrow if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll have to do one day without still but we'll survive that. It's appreciated that both parties agreed on giving this aid to the Chamber, and we're looking forward to receive it. Nothing else. Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. Mr. Usher, could you give the text to the witness. Would you please make that solemn declaration, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Popovic. Mr. Popovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Witness, for coming.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Following our normal procedure in the courtroom, would you please tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I am Radovan Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, was there a time when you gave a written statement to the Defence team of General Mladic and answered the questions that were put to you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to call up in e-court 65 ter 1D01752.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you will be able to see on the screen the text in a language that you understand, and in English, and I will ask you if you recognise the signature here.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we look at the last page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, on this page, can you identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How about the date, 12 July 2014, was it written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, when we were preparing yesterday and the day before for your appearance in the courtroom and when you reviewed this statement, would you now, after giving the solemn declaration, provide the same answers to the questions that had been put to you; and does this statement reflect a correct, faithful, and veracious picture of the matters discussed in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender the statement of Witness Radovan Popovic as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1752 receives number D1238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I should like to read a short summary of the statement of Witness Radovan Popovic. Witness Radovan Popovic is a journalist by occupation and in the course of 1995 he worked in the newspaper "Vojska," "Army," before becoming the head of the photo centre in the newspaper "Vojska." He worked together with a colleague, Ms. Biljana Djurdjevic, who asked him to record on a video camera her wedding scheduled for 16 July 1995. On that day, he arrived at her apartment at around 8.00 in the morning. He filmed the bride's preparation for the wedding. And, around 10.00 a.m., he filmed the arrival of the groom, Zarko, and his closest family and friends as well as the arrival of the best man and bridesmaid, Ratko and Bosiljka Mladic. After that, he also filmed the wedding ceremony at the church. And after that, they went on foot to the restaurant Two Fishermen, where there was a luncheon and a celebration of the wedding. Together with them there were the best man and bridesmaid, General Mladic and his wife, and they were constantly around and on camera. He filmed all the way up to 1700 hours when the VHS tape, 180 minutes long, was filled; and then having agreed with the young couple to go and buy another VHS tape, he briefly left. When he returned to the restaurant to continue filming, General Mladic and his wife were no longer there. Now, with your leave, Your Honours, I would like to put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please focus on paragraph 5, which is now D1238, a Defence exhibit. Mr. Popovic, when you see that statement and find paragraph 5, could you please tell us for the sake of precision, to the best of your recollection, when was the church wedding ceremony over and when did you arrive at the restaurant on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: The church wedding finished a little after 1.00 p.m., but we stayed at the porch of the church for another half an hour because the whole wedding party wanted to have their pictures taken with the young couple. There were also other rituals, like throwing the wedding bouquet over the bride's shoulder, et cetera. Then we moved on, and we arrived at the Two Fishermen restaurant around 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, how far is the restaurant from the church?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly, I would say 400, 500 metres. Not more than 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the wedding party walk there or go by car?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: We all walked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the best man, General Mladic, also in that procession together with his wife, who was the bridesmaid, Bosiljka?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: They never left the wedding party. They were always with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 6 of your statement. We should move to the next page. It's D138 [as interpreted]. Could you be more specific. This place that you refer to as Zeleni Venac where you went to buy another VHS tape, how far is that from the restaurant, Two Fisherman, where the luncheon was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Zeleni Venac, the square, is about 15, 20 minutes' walk from the restaurant, about 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the wedding was over, what did you do with those two VHS tape, with the whole film -- or tapes, rather?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: After coming back to the restaurant with the new tape, I inserted it into the camera and continued filming. From 6.00 p.m. to 10.00 p.m., when we left the restaurant, I had another hour of footage on that new tape; and - together with the newlyweds - I went to their home, where I filmed another half-hour of footage. When we all thought it was enough, I took out the tape from the camera, and - together with the first tape - I gave them both to the newlyweds and told them that it was my wedding gift to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have those tapes in your possession after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, was there the technical possibility on those tapes to put a time stamp on, the tape length, duration, and date?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I've filmed using my own camera, Panasonic M3000. It's a camera that uses VHS tapes. And the whole time that I filled, by default, in the right bottom corner there is a time stamp and the date, in the day/month/year format. In the top right corner of the display, the camera shows the whole time, how much of the tape has been used up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic, for these answers. These would all my questions for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You find Mr. McCloskey to your right. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see in your statement that you say that you left the restaurant at 5.00 p.m. to go get new tapes; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I said "5.00 p.m.," I meant perhaps five minutes earlier or five minutes later, but it's around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement says at about half past 5.00 or 6.00, unless I'm looking at the wrong statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We best look at the statement. Paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The tape ran out at 5.00. I gave myself a break and I waited for a convenient moment to tell the newlyweds. The first opportunity I got, I told them that the tape had run out and what they wanted me to do. I suggested going to the Zeleni Venac square to buy a new tape and continue filming. They agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just -- Mr. Stojanovic, in his summary, said 1700 hours. And I made a mistake when I said your -- the statement was at 5.00 p.m. but you then agreed with me and said it was 5.05 or maybe five minutes to 5.00 and then His Honour corrected us all. And so let's get real about this a bit. We can see from your statement that you first spoke to Mr. Dundjer on January 2012 about an incident that occurred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're on your feet. Do you want to intervene now or do you want to wait until Mr. McCloskey has formulated his question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid confusion on the record, because my short summary was mentioned. If we look at paragraph 5, the last sentence, it should be shown to the witness because it could cause confusion. And the problem is also what I said in the short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just that confusion that I would like to address the Court to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you should have refrained from making this comment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see that you talked to Mr. Dundjer and -- on 10 January 2012 and then on 12 July 2014. This is something we know happened in 1995, so many, many years after the fact. You've made a mistake, I've made a mistake. It's certainly possible, isn't it, sir, that you went over to that store to get a new tape maybe 30 minutes, maybe 45 minutes even, different than you've actually recalled?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How -- how can you be so sure after all these years, and you just fouled up the time when I asked you about it? You said it was at 5.00 when your statement says 5.30.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: The tape ran out exactly at 5.00 p.m. I remember that. I'm a photographer. I have photographic memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, Witness, would you carefully listen to the questions. If someone asks you: At what time did the tape run out? - you're supposed to tell us when the tape ran out. If you were asked: When did you leave the restaurant? - then you're supposed not to tell us when the tape ran out but then you're supposed to tell us at what time you left the restaurant. Would you please keep that clearly in mind in order to avoid any confusion. And perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, if you perhaps emphasise in your question exactly the time of what you're interested in, that might even prevent confusion to arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there other people taking photographs at the wedding?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: There was a photographer, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was that person taking still photos or video photos or both?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: He just took photographs, still photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while you were at the restaurant, did General Mladic ever leave your vision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, General Mladic did not leave the restaurant itself at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: While you were at the restaurant, did General Mladic ever leave your field of vision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. If I may, I would like to clarify and explain how that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a professional cameraman. When I set my camera, let's say I'm recording the guests dancing, as the camera is doing its work, I look around the hall, and I pay particular attention to the best man, matron of honour, and the bride and groom, so as not to miss an important detail or a custom or something of the sort. Hence, I kept the bride and groom in my field of vision as well as their best man and matron of honour, even when camera was not recording them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you're saying since the time you arrived at that restaurant, I think what you've said is roughly - what? - 2.30, until you left, at about 5.00, Mladic was in your field of vision the entire time, never left for a minute or two or five or ten?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we arrived in the restaurant around 2.00 p.m. For the next three hours, all that time, I had the bride and groom and the best man and matron of honour in my field of vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your photographic memory would have remembered General Mladic smoking and drinking?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, you are saying today in this courtroom, under oath, that General Mladic never excused himself for any reason, be it the restroom or some other reason that -- during those entire three hours?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so I take it you didn't use the restroom either?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, we have an intercepted conversation of General Mladic getting briefed by his Main Staff at 4.15 p.m. that day and he would have been on the telephone. And within a couple of hours after the restaurant that he was with you, he is also on the telephone being filmed by a video camera by some folks from Canada speaking about military matters. So go back to your photographic memory. If you, sir, were photographing or with General Mladic at 4.15, sir, I guarantee you would have seen him speaking on the telephone. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, you're a professional journalist. At the time you were for an outfit called "Vojska." That's "Army," right? What army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was the official publication of the General Staff of the armed forces of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Surely as the journalist you have heard about the massacres at the Branjevo farm that occurred all afternoon on 16 July while you were at this wedding. Had you heard about the massacres that have alleged to have been happening at the very time you were at the wedding, as a professional army journalist or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were things going on around Srebrenica in the course of those few days. I also know that many people died there, but I did not investigate or try to find out in detail about what had happened there. My editor-in-chief never asked me to do anything of the sort, nor did he ask any other journalist to do that. I might even call it taboo, a topic that was not discussed at the time. I do not recall any particular stories surrounding the Branjevo farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "things"? You say "things were going on around Srebrenica." Was that the professional jargon of journalists at the time for mass murder? What do you mean by "things"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is jargon. That's how I used the word "things." Horrible things happened there. Many people were killed. Many people died. Perhaps the term is not an adequate one, but that was the way I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you acknowledge that you have learned that the horrible things that happened were the mass executions of Muslims from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about it all much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So last question: Given that you were the professional journalist that was filming the Commander-in-Chief of the Main Staff, the commander of the VRS, the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and the man that's on trial for those murders that happened on the 16th, it never dawned on you to look into whether or not the man you were filming was a -- was -- or could be responsible for those murders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: That was not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Fluegge would have one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you were asked by the Prosecutor about Mr. Mladic at the wedding party, if he was drinking and smoking. Can you give some more details? What did he drink? How much and which kind of drinks?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic smoked some filter cigarettes, although I couldn't tell which. He drank mineral water. When he presented a toast, it was the only time when he had a brandy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many cigarettes did he smoke?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Many, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was he when he was smoking?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: He was seated at the table next to the bride and groom. Everyone smoked, including the groom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few more questions for you about the time. You said you ran out of your tape at 5.00. You also said that you then took some time off. What did you do then, when you did take some time off?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I had a cup of coffee and smoked a cigarette and then left to buy a tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you ran out of your tape at 5.00. A cigarette and a coffee would be how much time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And walking to the square, buy the tape, and come back, how much time was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Around 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of your previous answers was: "Zeleni Venac, the square is about 15, 20 minutes' walk from the restaurant, about 500 metres." Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It takes me 15 to 20 minutes to get there and the same time to go back. Let's say I need five minutes to purchase the tape and this brings us at around 40 minutes all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five hundred metres, that takes you 15 to 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not 20, 15 minutes, but then you need some time to find the shop. You also need to cross the street without any rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the time when you took a break for coffee and a cigarette, where were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was seated at a table which had been designated for the photographers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean still in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what the usual walking speed of a person is, on average? I mean, if you would normally walk, how many kilometres would you walk in an hour?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. It is 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- well, there's nothing to clarify, I think, for 4 kilometres. You say it's 4 kilometres. Now if it's 4 kilometres, then walking 1 kilometre would take you 15 minutes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If I would add five minutes for crossing the street to be cautious, lost, five minutes lost time, if I would then add five minutes for trying to find a shop - apparently you knew where the shop was or at least where approximately it was - and then how much time did you use in buying that tape?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Since it is one of the busiest streets in Belgrade, it is impossible to achieve a speed of 4 kilometres per hour. It's no jogging route. There are shop windows that draw your attention along the way. I was also looking for perhaps another shop where I could buy a tape. So I went from one shop to the next, and it was only at Zeleni Venac that I found a shop with tapes. I lost time and speed en route. I think it clarifies why it took me so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, all together, you were 50 minutes, approximately, away from the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe slightly less. It is difficult to tell you to the minute, but I was certainly away for 40 minutes, no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what you just told me a minute ago is that the tape ran out at 5.00, that you took a coffee and smoked a cigarette, not taking that much time. In your statement, I read that about half past 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon you agreed with the bride and the groom to go to Zeleni Venac neighbourhood. Earlier, when trying to find details, you more or less suggested that you would have left not later than quarter past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by my statement, that I left the restaurant at quarter past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your statement says different. Your statement says that it was about half past 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon that you agreed with the bride and the groom to go to Zeleni Venac. That's what your statement says. In court, you said that at 5.00 you took time for a coffee and a cigarette, which would take you ten to 15 minutes. Now which of the two is the accurate description of the timing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show me where it is where I said that I left the restaurant at half past 5.00 or 6.00? What statement was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to you: "Since the atmosphere was" -- paragraph 6 of your statement, which is before you on your screen I take it. "Since the atmosphere was nice and I did not have any more tape for recording, about half past 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon I agreed with the bride and groom to go to Zeleni Venac neighbourhood." So therefore, that must have been to agree that you would go somewhere, that's only possible before you have left, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: You are right, but then it goes on and it reads: "When I returned to the Dva Ribara to continue taping, it was around 6.00." It is possible -- it impossible that I would leave at 6.00 and return at 6.00. So I left at quarter past 5.00, returning just before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you had reviewed your statement and whether everything was accurate. You didn't say: I told something in paragraph 6 which is impossible; therefore, I want to correct that. You didn't say that, though given an opportunity to make any corrections you'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few. I need to clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, kindly direct your attention to the question put to you by the Bench, referring to the first sentence in paragraph 6. To the best of your recollection, at what time do you believe you bought the tape at Zeleni Venac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: At half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at paragraph 6, all of it, and while reading your B/C/S version, can you tell us what this reference to "half past 5.00 or 6.00" actually means?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I had in mind the time when I purchased the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slowly read the first sentence of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: "Since the mood was good and I did not have any more tape to record, about half past 5.00 to 6.00 in the afternoon I agreed with the bride and groom to go to Zeleni Venac neighbourhood and buy another VHS cassette in order to continue recording."

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say in your statement "half past 5.00 to 6.00," in your statement that you signed, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It refers to the time when I bought that other tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. On behalf of General Mladic's Defence, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you've described how conscientious you were and how important it was for you to tape these important things. Yet when the tape, as you say, runs out at 5.00, you kick back, have a cigarette, and it takes you a while to get back. So you missed quite a bit of -- of the party and General Mladic, I take it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wasn't General Mladic at the restaurant when you -- when the tape stopped and you started smoking?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you weren't taping from the time the tape stopped and the time that you got back from this shop with the -- with the tape. So you missed all of that good taping time; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: I missed the departure of the best man, and I was sorry about that, but it was not my fault. I didn't know the best man would leave so early.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It makes more sense, doesn't it, that you stopped the tape or the tape stopped after General Mladic left?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN POPOVIC
utterances.text: It would have been nice if it happened that way, but it wasn't -- it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have one question left for you. You went to the shop where you bought the videotape and you returned. You explained to us what made it relatively slowly for going that 500 metres one way, 500 metres another way. Now, did you slow down similarly on the way to the shops, still trying to find shops or not knowing where the shop was, or did you also on your way back to the restaurant take similar time looking at shop windows? I mean, was there any -- was going to the shop any slower than returning from the shop to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much approximately? I mean, what -- if you said you were away for 40 minutes, how much time did it take to you get to the shop and how much time did it take you to get back to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Stojanovic, has the -- have the questions of the Bench triggered any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Popovic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and also questions put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We went a bit beyond the usual time until the break. Has the Defence another witness on standby, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honour, no. As you know, the next witness and his proofing was conditioned by obligation towards the Canadian government, and at this moment our colleague Mr. Ivetic is working with the witness. He will be in the courtroom tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that we will not have a long session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have an agenda with quite a few administrative matters. We'd like to deal with those after the break. That will not take very, very long, certainly not a whole session; and after that, we'll adjourn for the day. Therefore, we'll take a break now. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges meanwhile have received the index of significant intercepted communications related to Srebrenica. There was another matter you would like to raise, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just so you know, this is most of the intercepts but some have come in at various times that came in after the book, but this is most of the Srebrenica intercepts and covers the significant -- most of the significant ones. In addition, there was one other matter that I owe you from a good while back. It was the -- back in the 18th of December, 2014, during the testimony of Milovan Milutinovic, a summary of a statement from the Dutch Institute of War Documentation came into evidence, and you strongly suggested it would be helpful if there was an audio it would assist the Court in reviewing the matter and the testimony. And so we took it upon ourselves to request the Dutch government to see if there was an audio, and to see if we could get that, and we are still working on that and hope to get a resolution very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive something from the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We received various communications and we're still working on it, or we're -- we've had a glitch here or two. So it looks like it's -- it's -- we're going to get an answer very soon, is what I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as you need the assistance of the Chamber in trying to get from the Dutch government which you think you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we actually sent them a transcript of your request so they knew exactly where it was coming from, from basically all of us here at the ICTY, the Defence, the Chambers, the Prosecution, so I think they understood, but I -- hopefully we'll be back to you with an answer very soon or a request for some help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it is now close to a -- nine months that you have not received what you requested. I would say if you could inform us within the next -- when in six weeks from now whether you have received anything, yes or no, because then it might be time to speed up matters and to see that at least we receive an answer within one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, for raising that matter. Then I'll start with the -- I would say the most urgent one which is about the expert reports of Mile Poparic and Zorica Subotic. On the 13th of May, the Prosecution requested the Chamber to exclude portions of three of the expert reports co-authored by Mile Poparic and Zorica Subotic prior to their testimony. As Subotic is due to testify next week, the Chamber informs the parties that it will deny the Prosecution's request and that it will differ its decision on admission of the three reports until after the witnesses have testified and a decision will be filed in due course. Then for the next item I'd like to brief move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. On the 26th of August of this year, during the testimony of Svetlana Radovanovic, P7513, a set of documents related to the exhumation at Sremska Mitrovica, was marked for identification and placed under seal, pending the provision of the complete English translation. This can be found at transcript pages 38323 to -330. On the 9 September, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and Defence via an e-mail that the complete translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID X019-4350-EDT. The Chamber wonders whether there's any objection to the admission of that new, now fully translated document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we'll be able to respond in a very short time, perhaps in a few days time before the end of the working week, if that suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to keep our agenda short, the Chamber already hereby instructs the Registry to attach the new translation to P7513 and admits P7513 into evidence under seal. The Defence has an opportunity to revisit the matter this week. The reason why we are proceeding in this way is because it's only the translation which is new, whereas you had already access to the document in its original language, Mr. Stojanovic. But, still, if there's anything in relation to the translation to be raised, you have an opportunity to do it this week. Then I move onto my next item which deals with the remaining issue from the testimony of Goran Krcmar. On 3rd of March of this year, P7171, an UN Security Council document, was marked for identification pending agreement between the parties as to the excerpt to be tendered. On the 20th of August, the excerpt was admitted as Exhibit P7171, and this is can be found on transcript page 38112 and -113. On the 24th of August, the Defence requested via an e-mail that two paragraphs be added to the exhibit. On the 9th of September, the Prosecution advised, again via an e-mail, that it had uploaded all excerpts, including the additional two paragraphs, into e-court as documents bearing Rule 65 ter 32099b. I take it, in view of the history, that there's no objection against admission, Mr. Stojanovic. The Chamber then hereby instructs the Registry to replace P7171 with the new excerpt of which I read a minute ago the 65 ter number. I move to my next item, which is a remaining issue from the testimony of expert witness Thomas Parsons. Pursuant to its notice of disclosure of expert reports related to the Tomasica mass grave dated 26th of August, 2014, the Prosecution tendered document bearing Rule 65 ter number 31088, which is an ICMP spreadsheet of DNA identifications. However, this document was not used during the witness's testimony on the 29th of June, 2015. If the Chamber does not hear from the Prosecution within seven days, the Chamber will consider this document to be formally withdrawn. Then I deal with the next item, which is a remaining issue from the testimony of Vinko Nikolic. On the 5th of February of this year, D893, a table of concordance listing the adjudicated facts included in Vinko Nikolic's witness statement, was marked for identification pending verification of the information contained in it. On the 27th of August, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution via an e-mail that a revised table bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05324a had been uploaded into e-court. Absent any objections from the Prosecution, the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current version of D893 with the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05324a and admits D893 into evidence. I now move to a remaining issue of the testimony of Dragisa Masal. On the 31st of March of this year, a press report from the "Los Angeles Times" concerning the shelling of Sarajevo, was marked for identification as P7233 pending a verification of its translation, transcript page 33385 to -390. On 28th of August, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber stating that CLSS stood by the accuracy of its original translation. The Chamber wonders whether the Defence has any additional submissions with regard to the admission of P7233. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I am unable to respond. I know there was an issue with the translation and, with your leave, I would kindly ask for some additional time until the end of this week to check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have time until the end of this week and a short message, either makes submissions or that there are no further objections, would do and we would then decide whether or not to admit this document. I now move to a remaining issue from the testimony of Mile Dosenovic, and it is about P7507. During the testimony of Mile Dosenovic on the 18th of August of this year, an audiotape was marked for identification pending the provision of the transcript of the recording and the related English translation. This can be found at transcript pages 37933 to -935. On the 10th of September, the Prosecution advised via an e-mail that it uploaded the transcript and the translation into e-court under doc IDs T001-1674-A-BCS and T001-1674-A-ET. Any objections as far as the Defence is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber hereby the Registry to attach the transcript and the translation to P7507 and admits P7507 into evidence. Then the last item on my agenda deals with the remaining issue from the testimony, again, of Mile Dosenovic, it's about P7508. On 18th of August of this year, P7508, an information report regarding the location of the former VRS Drina Corps command in Vlasenica, was marked for identification because the Defence disputed the determination of the elevation of a building as set out in the report and the B/C/S translation was pending. This can be found at transcript pages 37977 to -979. The Defence did not provide any further submissions despite the Chamber instructing the Defence to report back on the issue within three weeks. The Prosecution advised on the 28th of August, 2015, via an e-mail that it had uploaded the translation into e-court under doc ID 0687-4329-ET. Mr. Stojanovic, the question, of course, arises whether there would be any objections, also in view of the fact that further submissions were not made?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We sent the message to our associates to check these altitudes according to contour lines, and I believe we received an answer yesterday. By the end of the week, we will send you a short e-mail to inform you whether we agree with these markings regarding altitudes on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, I don't see whether can you see that on a map, but I think the main issue was the altitude or the elevation of the top of a building rather than any natural feature. But we'll wait for any submission you'll make later this week and leave the matter on hold. However, we already instruct the Registry to attach the translation to P7508 and we'll postpone then the decision on admission until we've further heard from the Defence. Is there any other matter either party would like to raise? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can get back to you on the Parsons exhibit, 65 ter 31088. That was one of the older spreadsheets. We dealt with updated spreadsheets in the testimony, so we can withdraw that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby on the record and it concerned 65 ter number 31088 and no exhibit number was yet assigned in any way, either to MFI or to do anything else. So therefore, that is now on the record, that the Prosecution has withdrawn it. If there's no other matter either party would like to raise, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 17th of September, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of September, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.25 a.m.,
